name: Annie Besant
role: British social reformer, Theosophist and Indian Home Rule leader (1847-1933)
summary: Annie Besant moved from Christianity to atheism and the Freethought movement, then to Fabian socialism, and finally to Theosophy and the Indian self-government movement. Across these phases she held to women's equality in law and marriage, free speech on religion, humane treatment of offenders and animals, and national self-rule within a reformed Empire. She opposed capital punishment, vivisection and meat-eating, and in India opposed Gandhi's breaking of laws.

Knowlton's own treatise, which she only published and was tried for; it states his views, not hers, and her own position is taken from The Law of Population.

The Law of Population (1877) argues that limiting births is the way out of poverty, but in the Autobiography she says she refused to reprint it after 1889 on Theosophical grounds. Because she explicitly and lastingly withdrew it, limit-population and population-causes-poverty stay null.

unions-good.rationale: Her own account in the Autobiography: she organised the Match-makers' Union (the strongest women's trade union in England), acted as its secretary for years, and organised the South London fur-pullers into a union.

women-suffrage.rationale: Her 1874 lecture On the Political Status of Women answers the objections to giving women the vote one by one; the 1925 Bill she helped draft says there shall be no disqualification or disability on the basis of sex.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Marriage pamphlet, chapter on divorce: an unhappy marriage should be easily dissoluble, since people who make a contract by mutual consent can unmake it, and incompatibility of temper is reasonable ground. Written in 1878 and not retracted in the sources reached, so medium.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Marriage pamphlet, divorce chapter: husband and wife must stand on perfect equality in asking for divorce, either side may seek it on the same grounds, and divorce by mutual consent is defended.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Marriage pamphlet: marriage should be a contract between equals and not a bond between master and servant, with marital control ceasing to exist and a wife holding the same property rights as if unmarried.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: Marriage pamphlet: loyalty of one man to one woman is the highest sexual ideal and monogamy is the result of civilization. She states it as an ideal, not as a legal prohibition, so +1.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Marriage pamphlet: she urges refusing legal marriage only while the laws remain immoral, and says the declaration should seek the law's sanction as soon as the laws are reformed; the law should enforce the contract's conditions and protect the children. Reformed legal recognition, not abolition.

civil-marriage.rationale: Marriage pamphlet: she proposes a simple public declaration, a written contract of partnership that should be stamped and registered when the law permits, in place of the present legal forms.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The Christian Creed (1883) attacks the blasphemy laws as persecution by bigots against free speech, and in her defence before the court in the Autobiography she calls them bad laws unfairly revived.

death-penalty.rationale: The Changing World (1909), lecture section on Capital Punishment: it cannot be defended by anyone who accepts Brotherhood, and the law teaches murder by punishing murder with death. The Basis of Morality calls it judicial murder.

rehabilitation.rationale: The Changing World (1909), section on the treatment of criminals: 'You should not punish, you should only help', train the prisoner in a trade, use probation for first offenders, and keep him until cured.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: The Changing World (1909): she rejects fixed sentences that grow longer after each return to freedom, and wants confinement only until the offender is trained and cured. This does not address the mandatory minimum itself, so -1.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: She denounces vivisection as the torture of the more helpless children of Nature (The Changing World), says in the Autobiography that she came to see it as fiendishly cruel and withdrew her earlier partial defence, and in her vegetarianism lecture refuses food that implies the slaying of or cruelty to animals.

animal-use-humane.rationale: Vegetarianism in the Light of Theosophy: she argues for abstaining from all animal food that implies slaying the animal, and holds that meat-eating degrades the slaughterers and is a moral responsibility on the eater. She does not discuss humane slaughter separately.

humans-entitled-to-use-animals.rationale: Same vegetarianism lecture and her condemnation of vivisection in The Changing World; she rejects both animal food and animal experiments, so she does not hold the entitlement as stated.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The Changing World (1909): whatever one has earned one holds as a steward and not as an owner, and wealth, education and power should be held as trusts for the common good.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: The Changing World (1909): wealth and power are to be held as trusts for the common good, and what one has earned is held as a steward, not as an owner.

class-collaboration.rationale: The Changing World (1909): liberty will never come 'by hatred of class against class'; she wants co-operation and profit-sharing and says the great change must come from above, not below. Her 1880s Autobiography stressed union of all workers against idlers, so +1.

religions-one-truth.rationale: The Changing World: Theosophy states the spiritual truths common to the great religions of the world, traceable in all scriptures, and she speaks of a real Brotherhood of faiths.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The Changing World (1909): 'in our education we must have religious teaching, in order that we may have a firm foundation for morals', on a broad basis common to the faiths. This is her later, Theosophical position; as a Secularist and on the 1888 School Board platform she stood for secular education, so this reverses her earlier view.

decide-locally.rationale: The Case for India (1917): the village decline can only be checked by re-establishing the Panchayat as the unit of government, and her aim was Panchayat, District, Provincial and National bodies built upward.

national-self-determination.rationale: The Case for India: 'the God-given Right to Self-Rule and Self-Development of every Nation'. She wanted self-rule as a dominion inside the Empire rather than a separate state, so +1 for the statement's 'state of its own'.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: The Case for India: 'Other-Government emasculates a Nation, lowers its character, and lessens its capacity'; Britons must give up the idea that India is a possession and treat her as an equal self-governing partner.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: The Case for India: 'Britons must give up the idea that India is a possession to be exploited for their own benefit'; India would have been richer and the Empire safer had she been a partner instead of a possession.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: The Future of Indian Politics: she broke with Gandhi in 1919 over passive resistance because breaking other, non-tyrannous laws seemed illogical and absurd and would breed lawlessness; she wrote articles on the sanctity of law.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The 1925 Commonwealth of India Bill she helped draft has a Fundamental Rights article and alters the constitution only by an absolute majority of both Houses after an interval (article 126). A joint convention bill, so medium.

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: The 1925 Bill (article 57): trials for offences against Commonwealth law 'shall ordinarily be by jury'. Joint draft she assisted with, so medium and +1 for 'ordinarily'.

separated-powers.rationale: The 1925 Bill's preamble: the Legislative, Executive and Judicial spheres 'shall be independent of each other' for the preservation of liberty.

communal-electorates.rationale: The 1925 Bill states 'there shall be no Communal Electorates', continuing reserved seats for Muslims and Europeans only as a five-year transitory measure; the Home Rule scheme she led sought one platform for Hindus and Muslims.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The 1925 Bill: all persons residing in the Commonwealth are equal before the law and have an equal right to use roads and courts, with no disability on the basis of sex; her 1874 lecture argues the same for women.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Autobiography: she gave her labour to the poor of her East End School Board district, urged feeding Board School children and decent housing for the poor, and said poverty is the result of ignorance and bad social arrangements that can be eradicated.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Autobiography, her 1884-85 Socialist writings: 'health, comfort, leisure, culture, plenty for every individual', 'enough for each of work, of leisure, of joy'. Stated as a social ideal, not as a guarantee by the state, so +1.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Autobiography, her 1884-85 socialist writings object to huge fortunes accumulated out of the toil of others; she does not state the full claim about profit from owning businesses.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The Case for India: she hopes the Government help given to munition factories in war will continue to industrial factories in peace, and blames the bureaucracy's laissez-faire for foreign takeover of India's mineral and dye industries.

arbitrator-settles-disputes.rationale: The Changing World: working to substitute arbitration for war is 'a great deal more practical' than nursing the wounded; she does not discuss whether arbitration should bind.

public-ownership.rationale: Industry under Socialism (1889): industries are to be run by municipal and national Boards, with communal councils reporting to a central Industrial Ministry as private enterprise dwindles. Her 1909 writing favours co-operation and profit-sharing without renouncing this, so the answer stays moderate.

local-essentials-public.rationale: Industry under Socialism (1889) treats gas works and tramways as run by the communal authority for its workers.

notes: First pass. Fabian phase: her 1889 essay Industry under Socialism supports communal and national ownership; her 1909 writing favours co-operation and profit-sharing without renouncing it, so public-ownership is scored moderately and other economic statements stay null. Her views changed across four phases: Freethinker and Republican (1874-85), socialist and Fabian (1885-93), Theosophist (1893 on), Indian Home Rule leader (1914-33). Where a later phase explicitly replaced an earlier one, the later view is used: she withdrew her birth-control pamphlet in 1889 (limit-population and population-causes-poverty left null), she wanted religious teaching in education after 1893 against her 1888 secular School Board platform (no-religion-state-schools), and she preferred dominion status under the Crown to a republic (monarchy-legitimate and elective-rulers left null because no source states her view). She opposed Gandhi's civil disobedience on the sanctity of law but left room for resisting a tyrannous law itself, so unjust-law-not-binding and civil-disobedience-accept-penalty are null. Themes searched across her books, the 1925 Bill, Britannica and the INC and Routledge pages: socialism and public ownership (her 1909 writing favours co-operation and profit-sharing, not state ownership; null), unions, education and school feeding, women and marriage, divorce, suffrage, caste, violence and revolution, empire and dominion status, religion and secularism, blasphemy, prisons and capital punishment, animals, population, nationalism, trade and industry, democracy. The record is thin on most of the bank's economic and technology statements, and failing the uncertainty rule is an honest result.
